title: fix(servicelb): pin the eBPF maps so a loader restart keeps flow state
description:
Route every map through EbpfLoader::map_pin_path so a loader restart reuses the
pinned maps instead of creating empty ones.

Today only links and programs are pinned, at src/main.rs:336 and :363.
Ebpf::load creates a fresh, empty map set on every start, and attach_and_pin
then calls bpf_link_update to swap the new program onto the existing pinned
link. The dataplane keeps forwarding, but against empty conntrack tables, so
every established flow breaks. In a DaemonSet that happens on every image
rollout, eviction, and OOM kill.

ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md line 133 already promises the
opposite: pinned under /sys/fs/bpf so restarts keep flow state.

Secondary win: during the swap the old and new map sets coexist, so peak
kernel memory is roughly double the steady-state 1.82 MiB. Reuse removes that
spike.

aya 0.14 supports this directly. EbpfLoader::map_pin_path routes each map
through MapData::create_pinned_by_name, which tries bpf_get_object on the pin
path first and only creates a map when the pin is absent.

DONE WHEN: a loader restart preserves conntrack entries, proved by a smoke
test that holds a connection open across a restart and fails if the entries
are lost.
notes: INVARIANT for Phase 5, from the 2026-09-05 review discussion: reconciliation (a Service/EndpointSlice change) is a live per-key write to VIP_MAP and POD_TARGETS via bpf_map_update_elem/delete_elem, per ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md:132 (load programs once, write maps on change, idle). It is NOT a program reload and NOT a process restart, so it never by itself resets the FWD_FLOW/REV_FLOW LRU conntrack maps -- those are separate kernel map objects untouched by a config-map write. The only things that reset the LRU maps are reload or restart with fresh unpinned maps, which is exactly the hazard this bead fixes. A well-built Phase 5 controller must never reload on a config change. Corollary: do NOT wire map auto-resize into the reconcile loop, since resize needs create-new-and-swap, which WOULD reset conntrack unless migrated.
close_reason: PR #1585 opened: pin eBPF maps via EbpfLoader::map_pin_path so loader restart reuses pinned maps and preserves FWD_FLOW/REV_FLOW conntrack; restart-preservation smoke test added and verified to fail on revert.

title: fix(servicelb): drop rather than forward a REV_FLOW miss on uplink egress
description:
Change the uplink-egress reverse-flow miss path from TC_ACT_OK to a drop plus
a counter, once the packet has been positively identified as backend traffic.

uplink_egress_return at servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:533 maps a failed REV_FLOW
lookup to TC_ACT_OK. On an LRU eviction the backend Pod's raw reply then
leaves the node unencapsulated, carrying a pod-CIDR source address onto the
underlay. That both stalls the connection and leaks a pod-source packet,
which is worse than dropping it.

The forward decap path already treats its equivalent miss as fatal:
geneve_ingress maps a failed try_geneve_decap_return to TC_ACT_SHOT. The
egress path should be consistent.

Care needed: try_uplink_egress_return returns None both for "not our traffic"
and for "reverse entry missing", and today both collapse to TC_ACT_OK.
Non-ServiceLB traffic must still pass untouched, so the two cases have to be
separated before a drop is safe. The POD_TARGETS membership gate bead
provides exactly that positive identification cheaply.

DONE WHEN: an evicted reverse entry produces a drop and an incremented
counter, with a regression test that fails if the fallback returns to
TC_ACT_OK for identified backend traffic, and unrelated egress traffic still
passes.
close_reason: PR #1624 opened

title: design(servicelb): flow-table admission control
description:
Decide how this dataplane admits a flow into the conntrack table before
anyone picks a max_entries ceiling, because table size cannot fix a table
that 8192 packets can cycle.

uplink_ingress inserts into FWD_FLOW at servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:238
immediately after the VIP_MAP match, with no TCP state check, no SYN gate,
and no validation of any kind. Any packet that reaches a service address
creates an entry, so an off-path sender can evict all legitimate flow state
with 8192 packets from varying source ports, which is milliseconds of
traffic. Sizing against expected legitimate concurrency does not help.

LRU never rejects, it evicts, so the failure is silent rather than loud.
Forward evictions drop return traffic; reverse evictions leak an
unencapsulated reply. Both are covered by sibling beads.

Research and decide among:

- Promote on evidence of bidirectionality. New flows enter a small
  unconfirmed pool and move to the main table only when the return direction
  is observed. Modelled on nf_conntrack's unreplied versus assured states.
  Protocol-agnostic, so one mechanism covers TCP, UDP, and QUIC. This is the
  recommended starting point if only one thing gets built.
- QUIC specifics. RFC 9000 section 8.1.2's Retry token is a first-class
  address-validation handshake. Better still, this dataplane already mints
  the DCID, so minting it with an embedded MAC makes every later short-header
  packet self-authenticating and prevents state creation outright. Note that
  draft-ietf-quic-load-balancers was declined at doc line 108 on routing
  grounds; the anti-flush property is a separate argument that was not
  weighed. RFC 9000 section 14.1's 1200-byte Initial minimum also raises
  flood cost roughly thirtyfold over a bare TCP SYN.
- TCP. A SYN gate is cheap but weak, since setting the bit is free. SYN
  cookies are the real analogue and need care in a load balancer that does
  not terminate TCP.
- UDP. No L4 signal exists at all: no flag, no handshake, no field
  distinguishing a first packet from a mid-stream one. The available levers
  are per-source-prefix rate limiting on state creation and per-service
  opt-in.

DONE WHEN: a written decision on the admission mechanism exists, and the
max_entries ceiling is settled as a consequence of it rather than guessed
independently.
notes:
DECLINED, with rationale, from the 2026-09-05 review discussion: runtime dynamic resize of the conntrack maps (scale max_entries up/down within a min/max range based on live traffic). Two independent reasons. (1) Economics: the table is ~120 bytes/entry (measured), so shrinking a tiny-cluster table from 8192 to 1024 entries saves ~860 KiB -- under 0.1% of a 1 GB node -- while the scale-DOWN direction a tiny cluster wants is the hardest to measure (silent LRU eviction, no live count). (2) Timing: a control loop reacts in seconds; a sudden burst (HN front page) saturates in milliseconds, so you cannot autoscale out of a burst -- by the time you detect+allocate+migrate+swap it has passed or already thrashed. Burst survival comes from graceful LRU degradation (never returns E2BIG, evicts LRU, self-heals on next packet, fixed footprint regardless of load -- cannot OOM from traffic) plus a pre-provisioned fixed ceiling plus admission control (this bead) to protect established flows from a flood of new ones. The legitimate-traffic burst and the malicious flush attack are the SAME mechanism seen from two sides. Right-sizing belongs at load time (discrete tiny/default/large profiles from node facts), informed by observability metrics (mayor-aie31.22), not a runtime swap. Corollary already on aie31.8: do not wire resize into the reconcile loop.
Findings doc: ai/findings/2026-09-06-mayor-aie31.11-flow-table-admission-control.md (branch worker/agent-aea30cb1ec81c8e99, commit 6a6cdbba). Recommendation: adopt option (a) promote-on-bidirectionality (nf_conntrack unreplied/assured, observable at ingress because symmetric return puts both legs on one node) as the mandatory protocol-agnostic foundation; ceiling derived as a consequence -> split FWD_FLOW into FWD_PENDING=2048 (only flood-exposed tier) + FWD_MAIN=8192 (unchanged but now justified). QUIC self-authenticating minted-DCID MAC (option b) conditional on g3lag choosing CID-based keying; reject TCP SYN-cookies (needs TCP termination). Couplings flagged: g3lag (anti-flush is a new argument for CID keying), aie31.21 (FWD_FLOW becomes affinity store; two maps must be designed jointly), aie31.20/aie31.17 (map substrate). Awaiting operator decision.
## critical-reviewer findings — findings-doc — mayor-aie31.11

**Verdict**: LGTM-with-suggestions

**Confirmed findings** (must be true, evidence cited):
- [MED] The core topology claim is TRUE: forward (`uplink_ingress`) and return (`geneve_ingress` VNI_RET) legs run on the same ingress node by construction, so the return-path `FWD_FLOW.get` at main.rs:514 genuinely is a bidirectionality proof. Evidence: `main.rs:246` inserts keyed on ingress-local tuple, `main.rs:431` (`RevFlowValue.ingress_node_ip = tkey.remote_ipv4`) captures the originating node, `main.rs:598` (`uplink_egress_return`) Geneve-redirects the reply back to that exact node. No fix needed — this confirms the doc's foundation is sound.
- [MED] The DONE-WHEN ceiling table splits `FWD_PENDING`/`FWD_MAIN` for TCP/UDP but defines no PENDING tier for the QUIC CID map, leaving the Answer's "closes...for TCP, UDP, and QUIC with one mechanism" claim structurally unbacked for QUIC. Evidence: doc lines 197-201 (table has only "Main (QUIC)", no "Pending (QUIC)") vs. line 14 and line 122 ("QUIC? Same — the first server response promotes the flow"). Suggested fix: add a QUIC PENDING/MAIN split to the ceiling table or explicitly justify why QUIC's CID map doesn't need one.
- [MED] Option (b)'s "LB mints DCID with embedded MAC" mechanism rests on the same "LB-minted CID" model that sibling finding mayor-g3lag (committed 12s earlier, same session, commit 78c738bf) explicitly refutes as unrealizable for a non-terminating dataplane under BOTH of g3lag's realizable keying paths — pass-through has no CID map, and QUIC-LB method 3 has the *backend* mint the CID, not the LB. Evidence: aie31.11 doc lines 152-161 ("this dataplane already mints the DCID... If it mints it with an embedded keyed MAC") vs. g3lag doc lines 222-225 ("the anti-forgery property comes from the backend's encrypted server_id encoding, not an LB-minted MAC... not off a MAC the LB stamped"). aie31.11's framing ("if and only if mayor-g3lag chooses CID-based keying") implies (b) becomes buildable as-written once g3lag picks CID keying; per g3lag it does not — it needs redesign to validate a backend-minted value, not describe minting one. Suggested fix: reframe (b) as "validate backend-minted QUIC-LB server_id" conditional on g3lag's method 3, not "LB mints DCID+MAC" conditional on "CID-based keying."

**Suspicions** (worth the maintainer's attention, but I did not confirm):
- The non-atomic PENDING get→insert→delete promotion sequence is claimed benign under all interleavings. Why suspicious: claim is asserted, not demonstrated against concurrent-CPU BPF map semantics. To verify: trace a concrete two-CPU interleaving (forward re-insert racing a return-triggered promote/remove) against BPF map atomicity guarantees, or defer to implementation-time review.

**Not reviewed** (out of scope for this deliverable's checklist):
- netfilter `early_drop`/`IPS_ASSURED` internals — doc itself discloses these are from established knowledge, not a fetched source.
- RFC 9000 §8.1.2/§14.1 text — not independently re-fetched; relied on general knowledge and g3lag's own overlapping RFC citations.

**Meta**: reviewed at 2026-09-06T09:44:31Z, deliverable size (1 file / 285 lines), checklist items checked (5/5 findings-doc checklist items: citation quality, verdict soundness, follow-on beads, uncertainty language, file location).

Overall: the mandatory recommendation (adopt promote-on-bidirectionality as the protocol-agnostic foundation) is sound, its topology premise is verified true against `main.rs`, and the fallback for QUIC under 4-tuple pass-through (option (a) + §14.1 size gate, no MAC) is real and matches g3lag's own conclusion — the operator can rely on that core recommendation. The two MED findings above affect only the DONE-WHEN table's QUIC completeness and the conditional/optional MAC layer, not the mandatory foundation.
DECISION (operator 2026-09-07): ACCEPT option (a) promote-on-bidirectionality as the flow-table admission foundation -- 2-tier, new flows enter FWD_PENDING and promote to FWD_MAIN only when the return leg is observed (protects established flows from a spoofed flood). Protocol-agnostic; QUIC uses the same (a) since g3lag chose tuple-based, so option-b DCID-MAC is NOT built for the MVP. CONSTRAINT (operator): the map sizes (FWD_PENDING, FWD_MAIN, and any per-protocol tier) MUST be CONFIGURABLE by the userspace DaemonSet at load time -- NOT hard-coded consts in the eBPF object. Implementation pending under the aie31 build phases; bead stays open as impl-ready.

title: fix(servicelb): POD_TARGETS holds one port per pod, breaking multi-port Services
description:
POD_TARGETS maps a pod IP to a single u16, so any Pod with two distinct
target ports is already mis-DNATed in shipped code.

servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:130 declares HashMap<u32, u16> keyed on pod IP
alone, with no port set and no protocol dimension. The forward decap reads it
at line 345 to pick the DNAT target port. One value per pod cannot represent:

- a multi-port Service, for example 80 to 8080 alongside 443 to 8443
- a Pod backing two Services, for example app traffic plus a metrics endpoint
- TCP and UDP on different ports

HTTP/3 happens to survive this. A Service declares TCP 443 and UDP 443 as two
port entries, because a Service port entry carries exactly one protocol, and
both point at the same target port. The map stores only the number, so one
entry serves both. That is coincidence, not coverage.

Wire-format wrinkle: widening the map is not sufficient on its own. The
forward Geneve option carries only the raw pod IP, per the settled decision
at ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md line 149, so the backend cannot
disambiguate two target ports for one pod. Either the option grows, or the
backend re-keys off what the packet still carries at decap time, namely the
VIP, the VIP port, and the protocol. That information is present and
sufficient, so the fix exists, but it is a design change rather than a
widening of the value type.

Blocks Phase 5, mayor-9gr0n, for a plain multi-port Service.

DONE WHEN: a Service with two target ports on one Pod routes both correctly,
covered by a test that fails against the current single-value map.

title: net/servicelb: implement bpftool map-memory + loader-RSS sampler (sample-ebpf-memory.sh) + CI wiring
description:
Implements the design in ai/findings/2026-09-04-mayor-aie31.6-ebpf-memory-monitoring-design.md (read it first -- this bead only restates the build steps, not the rationale).

Build scripts/servicelb/sample-ebpf-memory.sh, a standalone script (no dependency on scripts/conformance/*'s VM/workdir/kubeconfig conventions -- it must run unmodified against the Tier-1 smoke fixture, a bare CI runner, or a real fleet node):

1. Map discovery: for each `<pin-dir>/*-prog` pinned program, `bpftool prog show pinned <path> --json`, union the `.map_ids[]` arrays (dedup). For each id, `bpftool map show id <id> --json` and extract `name`/`type`/`max_entries`/`bytes_memlock`. Verified live on lima-node-smoke 2026-09-04: uplink_ingress-prog/geneve_ingress-prog/uplink_egress_return-prog union to exactly {VIP_MAP, CONFIG, REV_FLOW, POD_TARGETS, FWD_FLOW} (ids 189-193 in that run; ids are per-boot, do not hardcode).

2. Loader RSS: resolve pid via `pgrep -f <loader-bin-name>` (default `u7s-servicelb`, flag-overridable), sample `ps -o rss=`. Same "skip the tick's row, don't abort" contract as sample-run-metrics.sh's sample_one_host_process for a not-yet-started or already-dead process.

   - ebpf-map-memory.csv: ts,map_id,map_name,map_type,max_entries,bytes_memlock (one row per map per tick)
   - loader-rss.csv: ts,pid,rss_kb (one row per tick)
   ts format: `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` (matches sample-run-metrics.sh).

4. Two modes:
   - `once --pin-dir <dir> [--loader-bin-name <name>] [--out-dir <dir>]`: single snapshot, one call each to the CSVs above, exits.
   - `start --pin-dir <dir> --interval <secs> [--loader-bin-name <name>] [--out-dir <dir>]` / `stop`: background loop with PID-file idempotency, mirroring sample-run-metrics.sh's cmd_start/cmd_stop (SIGTERM + poll, disown, idempotent stop on missing/stale pidfile). Default interval 30s (matches sample-run-metrics.sh's default).

Print both CSVs' new rows to stdout at the end of the `run` case (`cat`), so they land in smoke.sh's own terminal output / CI job log with no new artifact-retrieval mechanism.

New CI job promoted from the throwaway `zz-ebpf-ci-spike` workflow (GH run 33882862825, 2026-09-04, litehop/u7s -- read its steps via `gh run view 33882862825 --log` for the exact bpftool-install + build + smoke-remote.sh invocation this job already proved works natively on ubuntu-latest in ~70s, no Lima/cross-build needed since the runner is amd64). title: net/servicelb: conntrack full-tuple keying + VIP/pod-identifier echo format
description:
Phase 3 of mayor-aie31 (ServiceLB implementation epic). Hardens Phase 2's
single-flow happy path into the real conntrack model from
ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md's "Conntrack & affinity" section:

- Forward (ingress) key MUST be the full tuple (CLIENT_IP, SRC_PORT,
  VIP_IP, VIP_PORT, proto) -- a client-only key collides across two
  concurrent connections from the same local port to two different VIPs
  that resolve to the same ingress node.
- Backend's reverse-flow key (CLIENT_IP, SRC_PORT, PodIP, TargetPort,
  proto) is rewrite-stable but not yet proven unique across flows -- see
  this bead's "resolve open questions" list below.
- BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_PERCPU_HASH, one map per protocol, sized per the
  doc's table (TCP: IPv6-primary 37-byte key, 8192-entry ceiling; QUIC:
  fixed-length DCID prefix key, 4096-entry ceiling).
- Extract the pure key-encode/decode logic into plain Rust functions
  (not embedded only in the eBPF program) so they are unit-testable
  outside a kernel (Rule 14 -- a conntrack keying bug is not verifiable by
  inspection alone).

Resolve the three open questions ebpf-lb-dataplane.md leaves unsettled
before this phase closes (pick one, document the choice in this bead's
close note, do not leave implicit): (1) Geneve option wire encoding --
pod identifier: raw pod IP vs compact backend-index; VIP echo: raw
VIP_IP:VIP_PORT vs a compact flow-id. (2) VIP-to-PodIP NAT placement --
DNAT on backend plus un-DNAT on ingress (reusing the ingress's step-2
write) vs both on the backend. (3) Backend reverse-flow key uniqueness --
two Services (different VIPs) sharing a backend Pod at the same
targetPort, hit by a client reusing one ephemeral src port across both,
collide today; likely fix is folding the captured VIP into the backend
key too.

Depends on Phase 2 (mayor-g7jh2) -- conntrack keying only matters once
real packets flow the path it hardens. Blocks Phase 4 (prototype gates)
-- the go/no-go RSS measurement needs the real (not single-entry) map
sizing this phase produces.

Risk: MEDIUM-HIGH -- collision-proofing and per-CPU LRU eviction behavior
under churn is exactly the failure class ebpf-toolchain-aya.md's verifier-
maturity caveat and the design doc's own flagged "verifier rejection
under churn/scale" risk point at.

Verification: unit tests for the extracted key encode/decode functions
(the two-Services-one-pod collision scenario above as an explicit test
case). 2-node Lima load test with concurrent/churning connections
checking for verifier rejection and correct flow-affinity survival across
LRU eviction pressure.
notes:
DECISION (2026-09-03, operator): Decision 3 backend reverse-flow key uniqueness resolved = backend source-port remap, ON-CONFLICT ONLY. Forward-leg write checks if the reverse key already holds a DIFFERENT front address; if so allocate a synthetic src port unique per (CLIENT_IP, PodIP, TargetPort), store it, un-remap on return. Reverse tuple then unique by construction, protocol-agnostic (closes UDP, no teardown needed); client src IP:port untouched on the non-colliding happy path. NOT per-flow SNAT (destroys real-client-IP-at-L3, ADR servicelb-ebpf-geneve-dataplane.md:14). NOT accept+mitigate (fails the UDP/DNS flagship). Exposure model corrected to node-IP: clients dial node-owned NODE_IP:SVC_PORT via DNS, any node is ingress, no floating VIP; VIP in docs = front address. Refs: ai/findings/2026-09-03-mayor-gjbov-geneve-wire-decisions.md Decision 3, ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md.
SCOPE (mayor, 2026-09-04): NO automated eBPF VM/load-test harness exists yet. Phase 2 (g7jh2/#1557) was hand-verified on a 2-node Lima by the dev; there is no reproducible harness, and the ebpf-build CI job runs clippy+fmt+build but NEVER executes servicelb cargo tests. Therefore pa0ze verification is scoped to: (a) extract the pure-Rust key encode/decode functions and unit-test them, INCLUDING the two-Services-one-pod-same-targetPort collision case and the backend src-port-remap-on-conflict path (operator Decision 3); (b) the servicelb-ebpf bpfel-unknown-none build must pass (verifier-compilability). The bead's '2-node Lima load test' gate is DEFERRED to Phase 4 (lrbvo), which already owns the real-fleet return-path + RSS measurement. Traffic/churn/LRU-eviction load testing still deferred to Phase 4/lrbvo. Sequencing: aie31.1 harness lands first (or concurrently), then pa0ze uses it. Supersedes the prior unit-tests-only note above.
HARNESS GATE READY + CAVEAT (mayor, 2026-09-04): aie31.1 Tier-1 smoke harness merged (#1565) = scripts/servicelb/smoke.sh --vm lima-node-5. This is pa0ze's verifier-accept gate. If your round-trip trips IP_RPFILTER, do not chase it as a conntrack-keying defect. title: net/servicelb: Geneve encap/decap on the symmetric-return path (single-flow happy path)
description:
Phase 2 of mayor-aie31 (ServiceLB implementation epic). Implements the
packet-flow mechanism in ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md's
"Packet flow" section end to end for ONE static VIP-to-backend mapping
(hard-coded or test-fixture map contents -- real Service/EndpointSlice
watching is Phase 5, not here):

Forward: ingress classifier matches VIP:PORT traffic, stamps Geneve
metadata (remote = backend node, fixed VNI, pod-identifier option) via
bpf_skb_set_tunnel_key, redirects to geneve0. Backend decaps, reads
VIP_IP:VIP_PORT off the still-untouched inner dst BEFORE rewriting
anything, rewrites dst to PodIP:TargetPort (src unchanged), forwards via
flannel's routing to the veth -- the Pod sees the real client IP at L3.

Return (per docs/decisions/servicelb-symmetric-geneve-return.md, NOT
DSR): backend's egress classifier Geneve-encaps the Pod's raw reply back
to the ingress node, echoing the captured VIP_IP:VIP_PORT. Ingress decaps,
rewrites src back to the VIP, routes to the client sourced as an address
the ingress node actually owns.

Naive/single-entry flow state is acceptable here -- collision-proofing,
sizing, and eviction under churn are explicitly Phase 3's job, not this
one's.

Depends on Phase 1 (mayor-g6u8s) landing the loadable skeleton. Blocks
Phase 3 (conntrack hardening) -- conntrack keying only matters once real
packets are flowing this path.

Risk: HIGH -- this is the core novel mechanism the epic exists to prove;
Geneve option stamping via bpf_skb_set_tunnel_key and the decap/DNAT
capture-before-rewrite ordering are both unproven in this codebase.

Verification: 2-node Lima VM topology (minimum to prove a real cross-node
hop; the real disjoint-subnet/NAT gate is Phase 4, not here). Packet
capture (tcpdump on geneve0 both nodes) confirming inner-packet integrity
and correct VIP/PodIP rewrite ordering across one full request/reply round
trip.
notes: Phase-2 design constraints surfaced by PR #1543 critical-review (pullrequestreview-5103230572): (1) TC_ACT_OK SHADOWING -- the Phase-1 skeleton attaches geneve_ingress_decap AND geneve_ingress_return as TCX ingress on the SAME geneve0 iface, both returning TC_ACT_OK (== terminal TCX_PASS; only TC_ACT_UNSPEC/TCX_NEXT=-1 defers to the next prog). On a node that is BOTH a backend and an ingress node, whichever link attaches first permanently shadows the other once these get real decap logic. Phase 2 MUST design an explicit hand-off (TCX_NEXT chaining) or merge the two ingress paths into one program keyed on the flow. (2) bpffs pin EPERM on a literal "." in the pin filename (memory lima-bpffs-pin-rejects-dot-in-filename-eperm) applies to Phase-2 MAP pinning too -- avoid dots in map pin paths.
close_reason: PR #1557 opened: Geneve encap/decap symmetric-return dataplane, single static flow, verified live on 2-node Lima with a full HTTP round trip

title: net/servicelb: survey how major L7 proxies -- Traefik, nginx, Envoy, HAProxy -- handle QUIC CIDs, decide conntrack keying method
description: L3 conntrack design-input survey feeding the QUIC keying decision: CID-based per draft-ietf-quic-load-balancers versus 4-tuple pass-through. Traefik, nginx, Envoy, and HAProxy are learn-from candidates for how they handle QUIC Connection IDs, not blockers -- if none cooperates with an LB-minted fixed-length CID, 4-tuple pass-through is an acceptable fallback with degraded affinity across QUIC connection migration. Stays on the aie31 L3 dataplane track; see the reframed Conntrack and affinity section in ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md. Not a hard precondition for Phase 3 -- the keying method choice can land pass-through first and upgrade later.
notes:
Findings doc: ai/findings/2026-09-06-mayor-g3lag-quic-cid-conntrack-keying.md (branch worker/agent-a028828cfd1214de9, commit 78c738bf, no PR per brief). RECOMMENDATION: ship 4-tuple pass-through QUIC keying now; treat CID-based keying as a later opt-in upgrade using draft-ietf-quic-load-balancers self-encoding CIDs, NOT the 'LB-minted CID' the mechanism doc describes. Central finding: 'LB-minted CID' is unrealizable by a non-terminating tc-bpf dataplane -- the routing CID is server-chosen (RFC 9000 §7.2) and post-handshake CIDs are encrypted; only cooperation model is backend-generated routable CIDs the LB decodes (QUIC-LB draft). Survey: Envoy=YES (server-side quic_lb generator, only cooperator); nginx/HAProxy/Traefik=NO (all terminate QUIC, no external routable-CID scheme). Backends are arbitrary pods u7s doesn't control + short header omits CID length (§17.3.1), so CID keying needs backend cooperation and is unavailable by default. Coupling: mayor-aie31.11's 'LB-minted DCID with embedded MAC' admission shares the same false premise -- pass-through keying removes that lever, pushing aie31.11 to its protocol-agnostic bidirectionality-promotion default for QUIC. description:
FLAGSHIP Phase 1 (operator GO 2026-09-01). Produce a committed, focused DESIGN DOC for u7s own eBPF DSR dataplane -- a draft the operator will then refine. Not code; not a lit review; a design.

Confirmed requirement: external-originating traffic that lands on the WRONG node must reach a backend on another node AND the backend Pod must see the REAL external client IP at L3, with nodes on DISJOINT subnets. Only DSR plus overlay encap satisfies this. Extreme CPU and memory efficiency is mandatory -- kernelspace, per-packet -- so zero-alloc datapath, cache locality, per-CPU maps, minimal instructions are design constraints throughout.

Operator decisions to bake in: (1) DSR SUBSUMES the shell-script klipper-lb-alike -- this dataplane IS the ServiceLB, design accordingly. (2) QUIC Connection-ID conntrack is a v1 requirement -- design the CID extraction and CID-to-backend affinity from day 0, alongside TCP 4-tuple conntrack. (3) Toolchain is OPEN -- survey aya vs libbpf-rs vs C-plus-libbpf and RECOMMEND one for the operator to decide.

Design doc must cover, each with a recommended design plus trade-offs plus any open question for the operator:
- Datapath and hooks: XDP ingress match-plus-redirect plus tc-bpf for conntrack access; the exact packet flow ingress-node matches VIP, selects backend, Geneve-encaps the client-to-VIP packet to the backend node, decap, Pod sees real client IP, reply.
- THE return-path crux: how the backend Pod reply is sourced AS the VIP and reaches the external client directly across disjoint subnets without returning through the ingress node -- VIP-on-loopback vs eBPF egress rewrite; whether the return leg needs encap. This is the mechanism the fhfro review flagged as unexamined; nail it.
- Conntrack and affinity: TCP 4-tuple-to-backend map; QUIC Connection-ID extraction plus CID-to-backend map (v1). Map types, per-CPU vs shared, LRU, sizing for under 10 nodes under 100 services under about 1000 endpoints, and the pre-allocation memory budget.
- Userspace control plane: minimal Rust watcher of Service type LoadBalancer plus EndpointSlice, populating maps; load-once then watch; memory-minimal.
- Toolchain recommendation (aya vs libbpf-rs vs C) weighing Rust-fit, CO-RE, verifier maturity, and QUIC-parsing-in-eBPF feasibility.
- Coexistence with kube-proxy and flannel (our CNI, docs/decisions/flannel-for-cni.md).
- Prototype gates to carry into Phase 3: return-path works across real disjoint subnets; measured footprint on a real 1GB node. Name these as the go/no-go gates.

Sources: bd show mayor-fhfro and mayor-mma08 notes (prior datapath sketch plus the critical-review caveats plus the live Lima kernel-7.0 eBPF-helper evidence), ai/findings/legacy/cni-svclb-landscape-2026-08-25.md, docs/decisions/flannel-for-cni.md, and fetch references via gh api or curl: aya, libbpf-rs, Katran, blixt (Rust-plus-aya k8s L4 LB, closest analog), Cilium DSR Geneve, kube-router tunnel-DSR, QUIC header format for the CID. Supersedes fhfro and mma08.
notes:
OPERATOR DECISION 2026-09-01: adopt the SYMMETRIC return-through-ingress-node model, NOT DSR. Reply path: pod->B->Geneve->A->client, A sources its own IP (no forging). Rationale: DSR return-offload benefit is nil at u7s scale (no video/download-heavy use case); symmetric eliminates source-spoofing/uRPF, the home-NAT-node exclusion, and the public-VIP requirement. Per-node public IPv6 /64 pools make symmetric VIPs clean (node-owned, uRPF-safe). Revisit DSR only if a download-heavy high-throughput workload arises AND provider allows cross-node egress source-forging. Revising the design doc now.
Critical-review of PR #1500 = needs-changes. 2 REAL defects to fix in the restructure: (1) HIGH -- the conntrack section claims one flow-affinity entry serves both directions via a full-4-tuple src/dst swap, but that is incoherent at the ingress return: step 2 stores key CLIENT_IP:SRC_PORT + VIP:PORT, yet the returning packet at step 7 carries PodIP:TargetPort (post-DNAT, pre-un-DNAT) on the non-client side, so a 4-tuple swap cannot match the stored entry. Fix: key the ingress lookup on the CLIENT 2-tuple (CLIENT_IP:SRC_PORT, proto), stable in both directions; the one-map conclusion likely survives but the KEY description and the no-separate-reverse-map footprint claim must be re-derived. (2) MEDIUM -- the TCP key sized 13 bytes is IPv4-only (4+4+2+2+1); the fleet is IPv6-primary per the landscape doc, so keys are ~37 bytes -- confirm the ~64B/entry footprint row accounts for IPv6-sized keys. CHECKED OUT: loxilb citation byte-accurate, no dangling fhfro file cite, footprint sums ~3.9-6.65 MiB, DSR risk-layer gone, kube-proxy-east-west faithful.

title: net: minimal Service LoadBalancer -- shell-script ServiceLB (klipper-lb-alike) with source-IP preservation (fix MASQUERADE bug)
description: THE network-stack priority once the csi-hostpath story wraps (operator, 2026-08-31: this is the big one). Reimplement/fork k3s klipper-lb: a shell-script that installs iptables DNAT rules with NO persistent proxy loop (install-rules-once-then-idle; the kernel does all packet forwarding, so per-instance cost is ~92KB RSS and fan-out across Services x protocols x nodes stays near-free -- preserve this design property, do not reintroduce a per-instance proxy process). Fix klipper-lb's one known defect: the unconditional POSTROUTING MASQUERADE in its entry script SNATs every packet regardless of externalTrafficPolicy, causing source-IP loss -- omit MASQUERADE when the destination is local. Verify end-to-end: source-IP preservation against a real backend for BOTH TCP and UDP (the operator's prior split-horizon DNS attempt confirmed the bug affects UDP too, not just HTTP/TCP); QUIC/HTTP3 UDP flow affinity (same 4-tuple must pin to one backend via conntrack -- confirm, do not assume); measured footprint under real connection churn (do not assume negligible -- loxilb's disqualification is the cautionary tale); correctness. Bundle as a u7s default the way kube-proxy is shipped (plain manifest + externally-editable image tag, NOT include_bytes into the binary). Reference: ai/findings/legacy/cni-svclb-landscape-2026-08-25.md (Service LoadBalancer section) -- loxilb disqualified (cannot start on 1GB), MetalLB/kube-vip ruled out for the WAN/Tailscale topology.
notes:
ServiceLB feature-decision refinements (operator, 2026-08-31), correcting the #1486 design doc: (1) NODE SELECTION is NOT a v1 requirement -- nice-to-have (MAY) at most, not the SHOULD-likely-promotes-to-MUST the doc claimed. (2) LAN-IP is NOT meaningless: the doc dismissed the home node private LAN IP as meaningless to an external client, but access FROM that LAN (a client on the home network hitting the LAN IP) is a REAL demand. LAN access is a requirement -- the LB must be reachable on the LAN IP AND preserve the LAN client source IP; do NOT prune the LAN IP. This also argues against node-selection being required. (3) SOURCE-IP / real-client-IP is CONFIRMED a hard v1 requirement (already MUST in the doc under externalTrafficPolicy=Local, TCP+UDP). Upstream status: source-IP preservation under externalTrafficPolicy=Local is a SPECIFIED Kubernetes Service API behavior (the defined purpose of the Local policy), with upstream e2e coverage (external-source-IP-preservation / ESIPP tests) -- a requirement, NOT incidental. The doc line source-IP loss is upstream-correct-not-a-bug applies ONLY to the Cluster DEFAULT policy (SNAT expected for even load distribution); it does NOT apply to the operator need, which Local serves. klipper-lb unconditional-MASQUERADE VIOLATES the Local contract -- exactly the bug this ServiceLB fixes. Still-open Qs: controller placement, SCTP v1, fork-vs-reimpl, IPv6 timing, label naming.
Design clarification (operator Q, 2026-08-31): client-IP loss under externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster is a HARD, inherent consequence of standard kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) SNAT -- NOT an incidental upstream limitation. Mechanism: Cluster may forward to a pod on a DIFFERENT node; without SNAT the pod reply routes directly back to the client, bypassing the entry node, breaking the connection (asymmetric routing / 4-tuple mismatch). SNAT rewrites src->entry-node so the reply returns symmetrically -- at the cost of the pod seeing the node IP. Deliberate L4 tradeoff (Cluster = even distribution + possible extra hop + client IP obscured; Local = client IP preserved + only-local-endpoints + possible drop/imbalance), documented + conformance-covered. Preserving client IP CROSS-node needs a different dataplane (DSR/direct-server-return, e.g. Cilium) -- out of scope for u7s (kube-proxy + shell klipper-lb-alike). IMPLICATION for operator scenario (Traefik as a Deployment, NOT DaemonSet): traffic to a node without a Traefik pod takes the hop -> Cluster SNATs (IP lost) or Local drops (no local endpoint). To get real client IP to a non-DaemonSet Traefik: (a) run Traefik as a DaemonSet + externalTrafficPolicy=Local (k3s pattern, no hop), or (b) recover at L7 via PROXY protocol / X-Forwarded-For -- which the L4 ServiceLB does NOT add by default. This RECONSIDERS PROXY-protocol-v2, listed as a v1 WONT: if a non-DaemonSet ingress must see client IPs, PROXY protocol becomes relevant. New open feature decision.
ARCHITECTURE constraint clarified (operator Q, 2026-08-31): requirement = cross-node delivery (request may target a Pod on a DIFFERENT node than the ingress node) + the Pod app sees the REAL external client IP at L3 (no app code change, no XFF/PROXY-protocol) + nodes NOT locally connected (no shared L2). This is the SNAT trilemma: cross-node hop + no-SNAT + working-connection is ONLY satisfiable via Direct Server Return (DSR) -- the backend replies directly to the client sourced AS the VIP, so the client connection matches and the app sees the real client src. Carrying the client->VIP packet across non-local nodes needs overlay encapsulation (Geneve/VXLAN/IPIP). Canonical impl: Cilium DSR mode (loadBalancerMode=dsr/hybrid, dsrDispatch=geneve, kube-proxy REPLACEMENT). kube-router tunnel-DSR (kube-router.io/service.dsr=tunnel, IPIP) is the other. Standard kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS) CANNOT do this: it SNATs on the cross-node hop; externalTrafficPolicy=Local preserves client IP but ONLY for local-node delivery (no cross-node). MetalLB/klipper-lb ride on kube-proxy -> same limit. IMPLICATION for 0gpqp: the planned klipper-lb-alike gives client-IP preservation ONLY for local delivery (Local + DaemonSet ingress, no hop); it architecturally CANNOT do cross-node + real-client-IP. If that is a HARD requirement, the ServiceLB must move to a DSR dataplane (Cilium-class) -- which cni-svclb-landscape DISQUALIFIED for the memory budget (Cilium OOM history; kube-router leak). Direct tension u7s footprint vs this requirement. Operator decision: (a) accept a DSR dataplanes weight, (b) relax to L7 client-IP (XFF/PROXY, needs app/ingress to read it -- contradicts no-code-change for the backend app), or (c) accept local-only L3 client-IP (DaemonSet ingress + Local, no cross-node). NOT resolvable within klipper-lb-on-kube-proxy.
close_reason: Superseded by the eBPF DSR dataplane initiative (operator 2026-09-01): DSR SUBSUMES the shell-script klipper-lb-alike. The klipper-lb-alike cannot do cross-node real-client-IP across disjoint subnets, which is now a confirmed HARD requirement, so u7s builds its own eBPF Geneve-encap DSR dataplane instead; ServiceLB is delivered by the DSR dataplane. lrqbx (Traefik ingress) now depends on the DSR dataplane for its LoadBalancer path. Design tracked in the DSR Phase-1 design bead.

title: net/servicelb: coexistence verification with kube-proxy and flannel (east-west untouched)
description:
Phase 6 of mayor-aie31 (ServiceLB implementation epic). Proves the
consequence docs/decisions/servicelb-ebpf-geneve-dataplane.md states but
does not itself verify: kube-proxy stays unmodified for east-west
ClusterIP/NodePort traffic, and this dataplane owns north-south
LoadBalancer VIP:PORT traffic only, with no double-processing between
the two and no flannel address-space collision.

Checks to run against a controller-driven system (Phase 5, not static
fixtures): the tc-bpf ingress classifier on the physical uplink never
matches ClusterIP/NodePort traffic, only LoadBalancer VIP:PORT; the VIP
address range sits outside flannel's pod-CIDR and Service-CIDR, and
geneve0 never touches flannel's vxlan device, confirmed live, not just
by address-range inspection; the one legitimate contact point, backend
decap handing its DNAT'd packet to flannel's pod-CIDR routing for the
last hop, behaves correctly under concurrent east-west and north-south
traffic on the same node; kube-proxy's existing iptables/IPVS rules and
this dataplane's tc-bpf hooks do not fight over the same traffic class.

Depends on Phase 5 (mayor-9gr0n): needs a controller-driven system with
real Service objects of both kinds (ClusterIP and LoadBalancer)
coexisting, not Phase 2's single static VIP fixture. Blocks Phase 7
(conformance gating): conformance runs assume east-west correctness is
already proven, not concurrently discovered.

Risk: MEDIUM. Mostly an integration-verification phase; the failure
mode (a routing rule ordering bug that lets the two dataplanes double
process or misclassify a packet) is a regression in EXISTING east-west
behavior, which the project's conformance suite already gates, raising
the cost of a miss.

Verification: Lima cluster running flannel plus kube-proxy plus this
dataplane together; existing ClusterIP/NodePort conformance-relevant
paths unaffected, confirmed via the existing e2e-focus suite, while a
type=LoadBalancer Service concurrently exercises the new path.

title: servicelb-ebpf: inbound Geneve-decap delivery must validate target pod against local serving-set to bound cross-node drift to a safe drop, not a misdelivery
description:
try_geneve_decap_forward (crates/servicelb/servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:331-471), the
backend/delivery node's inbound decap path, trusts the pod_ip stamped into the Geneve
option by the ingress node and DNATs to it unconditionally. Its only membership check,
TARGET_PORTS.get(VipKey{vip_ip,vip_port,proto}) (main.rs:361-368), is keyed on the front
tuple only -- it confirms this node hosts SOME backend for the front, never that the
specific pod_ip in the packet is a pod CURRENTLY serving that front on this node. There
is no analogue of aie31.14's egress POD_TARGETS-membership gate on this inbound path.

Why it matters (mayor-1dwwz cross-node convergence review of aie31.21): each node's
userspace controller processes the same EndpointSlice event at a different wall-clock
time (uplink latency), so per-node eBPF state can drift apart for multiple seconds. A
lagging ingress node can replay a stale FWD_FLOW pin carrying a departed pod's IP. If
that IP is reused by a new pod on the backend node before the lagging ingress evicts its
pin, today's code delivers the packet to the NEW pod -- misdelivery to a live, unrelated
workload, not a bounded drop/hang. The drift window directly widens the exposure.

Fix direction: before the DNAT+deliver in try_geneve_decap_forward, gate on a node-local
map keyed on (front tuple, pod_ip) -> current-membership, populated by this node's OWN
EndpointSlice watch (lag-free for its own local pods), and TC_ACT_SHOT if pod_ip is not
a current member. This makes the delivery node -- not the ingress node -- the
authoritative consistency point: ingress-side drift then degrades to a drop at the
boundary, never a cross-pod leak.

DONE WHEN: try_geneve_decap_forward rejects a packet whose Geneve pod_ip is not in the
backend node's current local serving-set for that front, with a regression test that
fails if the check is removed/bypassed, and live flows to still-serving pods are
unaffected.

Cross-refs: aie31.21 (crates/servicelb affinity+eviction findings doc, this bead is a
follow-on to its cross-node-convergence section) and aie31.14 (the egress-side
POD_TARGETS membership gate this inbound gate mirrors, on the opposite hook).

title: net/servicelb: prototype go/no-go gates -- real-fleet return-path + RSS measurement
description:
## CURRENT STATE (2026-09-08) — distilled; full journaling in notes below

Phase-4 go/no-go, 3 gates:
- GATE 2 (RSS/memory): effectively PASS. ~1.82 MiB/node conntrack maps (LRU_HASH preallocates 8192 entries -> constant cost, ~0.18% of 1 GiB). Lima-measured; sampler tooling landed (tk4ku/aie31.6).
- GATE 3 (monitorability): satisfied by the landed bpftool/RSS sampler.
- GATE 1 (cross-node symmetric-return round-trip): IN PROGRESS, NOT operator-blocked for the MVP. Tiered scope: TIER 1 = 2 Lima VMs over WireGuard (local, dual-stack) = the MVP; TIER 2 = 2 public-IP cloud nodes (operator provisioning); TIER 3 = 3-node incl NAT-home + IPv6-only (deferred). tc-bpf attach to an L3-only WireGuard iface WORKS (verifier accepts, all 3 progs attach). Round-trip not yet proven; two LOCAL blockers (neither needs external infra): (1) aie31.5 -- servicelb-ebpf hard-codes ETH_HLEN=14 and no-ops on an L3 wg uplink (code fix, prerequisite); (2) wg data-plane session would not come up on the Lima guest (wg set/show OK, no UDP listen socket) -- NOT the kernel (operator runs 4 physical nodes on that exact kernel over Tailscale), a local netns/Lima-config issue to diagnose with evidence.

NEXT STEP (highest value, operator-directed 2026-09-08): build+validate the Tier-1 2-Lima-over-WireGuard multi-node setup (aie31.7, incorporating the aie31.5 fix), proving the cross-node round-trip -> closes Gate 1 -> unblocks Phase 5 (9gr0n).

## ORIGINAL DEFINITION
Phase 4 of mayor-aie31: validation checkpoint (not new mechanism) running the 3 prototype go/no-go gates from ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md before scaling investment. Depends on Phase 3 (pa0ze, closed); blocks Phase 5 (9gr0n). Verification is live-measurement only (bpftool + OS RSS + an actual client->VIP->cross-node-backend->client round trip).
notes:
Clarification spike verdict (read-only, no VM run): PARTIAL -- 2 disjoint Lima networks do NOT fully satisfy gate 1 as-is, but the plan's stated reason overstates the blocker.

(a) Disjoint L3 subnets: Lima CAN provide this. user-v2-workers-a vs user-v2-workers-b are genuinely separate DHCP-assigned subnets / separate L2 segments (scripts/conformance/lima-start.sh comments L92-98, L986-987: 'Separate Lima networks are separate L2 segments with no path between them'). The plan's justification for 'Lima cannot substitute' (ebpf-lb-dataplane.md gate 1: 'none of the disjoint-subnet/NAT conditions...occur on a single-VM L2') is scoped to ONE VM's flat network -- it does not address, and does not rule out, 2 VMs on 2 disjoint Lima networks. That specific justification is imprecise as written.

(b) NAT/asymmetric path between them: HARD BLOCKER today, not fundamental. add-node.sh/lima-start.sh's inter-node route loop explicitly hard-fails cross-network pairing: 'no L2 path exists between separate Lima networks, refusing to program an unreachable route' (lima-start.sh ~L994-997). Zero built-in connectivity exists between user-v2-workers-a and -b right now. A manual NAT/relay bridging the two networks' daemons (both run on the same Mac host) is theoretically constructible but does not exist in this codebase and is unbuilt/unverified.

(c) Even if built, FIDELITY LIMITATION: a hand-rolled Mac-hosted relay only proves the Geneve mechanism crosses SOME NAT hop -- not the real Linode/Scaleway/home-router+Tailscale fleet's provider-specific behavior (real anti-spoof/uRPF, real NAT-traversal under real NAT types, real cross-provider latency/MTU) that the plan's open question is actually about (real-FLEET sign-off, not just a mechanism smoke test).

Gate 2 (RSS = resident memory, NOT NIC hardware -- no RSS/NIC-queue requirement exists anywhere in this Phase) needs NO real fleet at all: already Lima-provable, and precedent proves it -- loxilb's memory floor was measured on exactly a 1GB/1vCPU Lima VM (cni-svclb-landscape.md). Plan doesn't claim gate 2 needs real infra; only gate 1 is flagged Lima-insufficient, correctly for the reasons in (c) but overstated for (a)/(b).

Minimal next step: a live 2-VM test (user-v2-workers-a + -b, with or without a manual NAT relay) was NOT run in this spike -- next-session follow-up, not guessed here. Even if it passes, real-fleet gate 1 sign-off per (c) still stands as a separate operational requirement.
CLARIFICATION 2026-09-04 operator-confirmed: Phase 4 deploys the eBPF WITHOUT the Phase-5 DaemonSet -- which by construction cannot exist yet, since this bead BLOCKS Phase 5 mayor-9gr0n. Deployment for the go/no-go gate = run the Phase-1 loader binary from mayor-g6u8s build/load wiring, already CLOSED, MANUALLY on each real fleet node via ssh, populating STATIC fixture map contents Phase-2 style and sized per Phase 3. No dynamic Service/EndpointSlice watching and no managed per-node lifecycle are needed for a hand-run prototype measurement -- those are exactly what the Phase-5 DaemonSet mayor-9gr0n adds for production, and are useless before this gate proves the mechanism survives real-fleet NAT and RSS. So there is NO circular dependency: loading is available from Phase 1 onward, independent of the DaemonSet. The open operational dependency is real-fleet ACCESS -- ssh to the Linode/Scaleway/home-NAT nodes -- not a missing deployment mechanism.
PHASE-4 GATE-1 PREREQS 2026-09-04 researcher-confirmed (operator asked, preparing fleet ahead). REACHABILITY: both nodes need BIDIRECTIONAL IP reachability to each other, but NOT public routability -- a Tailscale/WireGuard overlay supplies the path. One-way NAT-initiate-only does NOT suffice: symmetric-return requires the backend to send the return Geneve packet back to the ingress node. Docs: servicelb-symmetric-geneve-return.md L16-52, ebpf-lb-dataplane.md L16 and L45-71. IP FAMILY: IPv6-only nodes fully supported for BOTH ingress and backend -- Geneve underlay supports IPv6 per RFC 8926, aya tc-bpf via bpf_skb_set_tunnel_key, conntrack key already sized for IPv6 at 37 bytes; Scaleway IPv6-only is an explicit target. A fully IPv6-only node is acceptable. TODO when g7jh2/#1557 lands: verify the Phase-2 packet code has no AF_INET-only assumption. LIMA AS ONE NODE: a mixed 1-Lima + 1-real-cloud-over-Tailscale topology is MECHANISM-sufficient ONLY -- it loses real-fleet fidelity on uRPF/anti-spoof, real NAT traversal, and cross-provider latency/MTU -- so fine for early mechanism validation but NOT for operator production sign-off, which gate-1 requires on REAL disjoint subnets. MINIMAL FLEET: 3 real nodes over Tailscale ideal -- Linode dual-stack, Scaleway IPv6-only, home-NAT dual-stack; a 2-real minimum Linode+home-NAT loses IPv6-only and cross-provider coverage. Per-node prereqs: u7s control plane + kubelet + Flannel; manual-ssh Phase-1 loader deploy from g6u8s; Phase-3 pa0ze map sizing must land first; Tailscale client per node with cluster reachable over the tailscale0 100.64.0.0/10 interface.
PHASE-4 SCOPE REVISED (operator 2026-09-04) -- supersedes the earlier PHASE-4 GATE-1 PREREQS note's IPv6-only-required + 3-node-ideal framing for MVP purposes. (1) IPv6-only is DESCOPED from the gate-1 MVP blocker: IPv6 was never tested at all, so gating the core symmetric-return mechanism on an untested IP-family axis risks an IPv6-specific issue masquerading as a mechanism failure. Prove the mechanism on dual-stack/IPv4 FIRST; IPv6-only becomes a SEPARATE follow-on, not a gate-1 blocker. (2) Tailscale/WireGuard is NOT a blanket requirement -- only needed if a node lacks a publicly routable IP (the home-NAT case). Two public-IP nodes peer directly, no overlay. (3) Operator insight: if an overlay is in the path anyway, two LIMA VMs over WireGuard/Tailscale test the same cross-node symmetric-return path as cloud nodes -- so the MECHANISM MVP needs NO external fleet access, removing the operational blocker. REVISED TIERING: TIER 1 (MVP, dispatchable, no external access): 2 Lima VMs over WireGuard, dual-stack, prove symmetric-return round-trip cross-node. CAVEAT to verify while scoping tier 1: our tc-bpf Geneve path must attach cleanly to a WireGuard tun interface (no L2 header, unlike a real NIC). TIER 2 (real-internet fidelity, needs 2 public-IP cloud nodes = operator provisioning): Geneve over real paths -- real MTU/PMTU, provider uRPF/anti-spoof, real NAT. TIER 3 (full fidelity, deferred): the original 3-node incl. NAT-home + IPv6-only Scaleway. Still downstream of pa0ze (map sizing). Next step (operator to greenlight): a tier-1 Lima-over-WireGuard spike bead.
OPERATOR DIRECTIVE 2026-09-04: greenlit trying TIER 1 (WireGuard-over-Lima) FIRST. Fallback: if WireGuard-over-Lima proves impossible, operator provisions VPS nodes -- and then Tailscale is needed to avoid the reciprocal-public-routability requirement between the VPS. Feasibility spike dispatched (plumbing-only, independent of pa0ze) -- verdict recorded here as POSSIBLE/IMPOSSIBLE.
WIREGUARD-OVER-LIMA SPIKE VERDICT: IMPOSSIBLE (as currently coded) -- mechanically POSSIBLE, functionally blocked. wg-tun tc-bpf attach: PASS -- created a real wg-type netdev (link/none, ARPHRD_NONE, no L2) in an isolated netns on lima-node-smoke and pointed the actual servicelb-ebpf loader's --uplink-iface at it; verifier accepted uplink_ingress/uplink_egress_return/geneve_ingress and all 3 attached as TCX links (confirmed via bpftool net list: 'wg-node0(2) tcx/ingress uplink_ingress', 'wg-node0(2) tcx/egress uplink_egress_return', 'geneve-wgspike(3) tcx/ingress geneve_ingress') -- kernel-level attach to a no-L2 device is not the blocker. Cross-wg round-trip: NOT COMPLETED -- couldn't get an actual WireGuard data-plane session up on this guest's kernel (7.0.0-30-generic): 'wg set <if> listen-port N ...' returns success and 'wg show' reports the config back, but no UDP socket for that port ever appears in /proc/net/udp or /proc/net/udp6 in either root or a custom netns, and tcpdump on the underlay veth captured zero packets during a ping across the tunnel -- looks like an environment/kernel quirk unrelated to the eBPF question, not investigated further given budget. Specific blocker (found by reading crates/servicelb/servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs, not just inferred): uplink_ingress and try_uplink_egress_return hard-code ETH_HLEN=14 and unconditionally read the EtherType at ctx.load::<u16>(12) then index the IPv4 header at ETH_HLEN-relative offsets -- this assumes every uplink-ingress packet carries a real 14-byte Ethernet header. A WireGuard interface is L3-only (confirmed empirically: 'ip -d link show wg-node0' -> link/none) and delivers packets with NO such header, so on a real wg uplink ctx.load::<u16>(12) reads into the middle of the real IP header (bytes 12-13 = the first two bytes of the source IP), essentially never equals 0x0800, and uplink_ingress falls through to TC_ACT_OK on every single packet -- the VIP redirect logic never fires, so nothing is intercepted; the dataplane would silently no-op on a wg uplink today, not crash or reject at load time. One-line: this does NOT clear tier-1 MVP as-is for a WireGuard uplink, but it is a small, well-understood eBPF code fix (make the L2-header skip conditional/absent for L3-only uplinks), not a kernel/infra limitation -- the operator does not need to provision VPS nodes to prove the mechanism; the mayor should route a code fix to whoever owns servicelb-ebpf (currently pa0ze, per this spike's brief) before the next smoke run, then re-run this same fail-fast attach check to confirm the fixed parse path also attaches+works on wg. Guest fixture fully torn down (netns/veth/wg devices/bpf pins/scratch files removed, wireguard module unloaded, lima-node-smoke's original 7-interface topology and bpf prog list confirmed unchanged post-cleanup).

GATE 1 TIER-1 STATUS (2026-09-08, aie31.5/aie31.7, PR #1619): NOT YET PROVEN end-to-end -- but 2 of 3 local blockers are now resolved with evidence, and a NEW, more specific blocker was found and isolated.

title: servicelb-ebpf: bpf_redirect fails crossing L3-only wg0 uplink into Ethernet-type geneve0 device
description:
Discovered while proving aie31.7's 2-Lima-WireGuard cross-node round trip (after the wg-session issue and aie31.5's L2-header-skip fix were both resolved). uplink_ingress/try_uplink_egress_return correctly classify a real client SYN arriving on a WireGuard (L3-only, ARPHRD_NONE) uplink -- confirmed via a live FWD_PENDING dump showing a correctly-decoded 5-tuple -- but the subsequent bpf_redirect(geneve_ifindex, 0) that hands the packet to geneve0 (always Ethernet-type/ARPHRD_ETHER) for encapsulation is dropped INSIDE THE KERNEL, not by the eBPF verifier or program logic.

EVIDENCE: `sudo trace-cmd record -e skb:kfree_skb` during a client attempt shows the encapsulated SYN freed at `location=__bpf_redirect+0x220 reason: NOT_SPECIFIED` on the napi/wg0 receive softirq. Corroborated by `ip -s link show geneve0`: TX `dropped` counter increments by exactly 1 per client attempt, with 0 corresponding RX on the peer node's geneve0/wg0 -- the packet never leaves the ingress node at all. The same veth-sourced (Ethernet-type) redirect to geneve0 works fine (scripts/servicelb/smoke.sh passes), so this is specific to the SOURCE device being L3-only (no L2 header, hard_header_len=0) while the REDIRECT TARGET (geneve0) is Ethernet-type and presumably expects a mac header the L3-sourced skb never carries.

Reproduction: `scripts/servicelb/smoke-wg-2node.sh --vm-a lima-node-2 --vm-b lima-node-4` (or any 2 Lima VMs on the same network) -- runs to this exact failure point automatically and prints the same evidence via its dump-evidence step.

Likely fix directions (not yet attempted, needs its own investigation): synthesize a minimal/dummy L2 header on the skb (e.g. via ctx.adjust_room with BPF_ADJ_ROOM_MAC) before redirecting from an L3-only uplink into geneve0, on both the forward (uplink_ingress) and return (try_uplink_egress_return) redirect sites. Also note: if a real L2 header ever needs synthesizing on encap, the DECAP side's inner-packet parsing (try_geneve_decap_forward/_return, still hard-coded to ETH_HLEN=14 per aie31.5's design note) may need matching review, since a WireGuard-sourced forward leg would then have to carry a real 14-byte header end-to-end through the Geneve payload for that assumption to keep holding.

title: design(servicelb): per-flow backend affinity pinning + endpoint-removal conntrack eviction (Phase 5)
description:
Phase 5 needs one coherent decision on flow-to-backend affinity: the forward
path must pin a backend per flow rather than re-resolving VIP_MAP per packet,
AND endpoint removal must selectively evict the conntrack entries that point
at the departed pod. These pull in opposite directions and cannot be designed
separately.

Two problems, one decision:

1. No per-flow backend affinity. uplink_ingress chooses the backend from
   VIP_MAP on every forward packet at servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:227, and
   FWD_FLOW only records which node the packet went to for the return-path
   existence check at line 496, where the value is read and discarded (see
   aie31.20). With today's one-static-backend fixture this is invisible. With
   real multi-endpoint Services in Phase 5, repointing a VIP mid-connection
   immediately moves live traffic to a backend that holds no TCP state for
   it, breaking the connection. Real load balancing needs the backend chosen
   once per flow and stored in conntrack, with later packets following the
   stored choice. That is what conntrack affinity is for, and the current
   shape does not do it.

2. No selective eviction on endpoint removal. When a pod leaves the
   EndpointSlice, established flows pinned to it are orphaned. kube-proxy
   actively flushes conntrack for a removed endpoint, which matters most for
   UDP, which has no teardown to age the entry out. The eBPF equivalent is a
   targeted pass that deletes FWD_FLOW and REV_FLOW entries pointing at the
   removed pod. This is a deliberate scoped delete, not a reset, and it is
   missing.

The tension: affinity pinning says do NOT disturb a live flow on an unrelated
config change, while eviction says DO disturb the specific flows whose
backend is gone. The decision has to state exactly which config changes
disturb which flows, mirroring kube-proxy's terminating-endpoint and
graceful-termination semantics.

Invariant this rests on, now recorded in aie31.8: reconciliation is a live
per-key map write to VIP_MAP and POD_TARGETS, NOT a program reload or a
process restart, so it never by itself resets the LRU conntrack maps. The
orphaning above is semantic, not a map reset.

Overlaps aie31.10, since keying the eviction pass needs a richer POD_TARGETS
than one port per pod. Phase 5 scope, mayor-9gr0n.

DONE WHEN: a written decision defines the per-flow affinity model and the
exact set of config changes that trigger selective conntrack eviction, with
UDP called out explicitly.
notes:
Findings: ai/findings/2026-09-06-mayor-aie31.21-affinity-pinning-eviction.md (pushed on worker/agent-a86241176a94239ea, no PR). RECOMMENDATION: stored per-flow affinity -- FWD_FLOW pins the full backend identity (backend_node_ip + pod_ip), chosen once on the first-packet miss via a deterministic hash over the ready set; later packets follow the pin instead of re-resolving VIP_MAP. Pair with scoped event-driven eviction on endpoint removal: UDP delete of FWD_FLOW pins to the departed pod is MANDATORY (no teardown; one-way UDP refreshes LRU forever), TCP self-heals via reset (delete optional/cleanliness), REV_FLOW deleted for BOTH protocols on the pod's host node to close the pod-IP-reuse hazard. Reconcile rule: only removal of the specific endpoint a flow is pinned to disturbs that flow; add/terminating-but-serving/policy/topology never evict -- mirrors kube-proxy's UDP-only CleanStaleEntries. COUPLING: conflicts with aie31.20 (affinity keeps FWD_FLOW alive -- re-scope .20 to the return-auth MAC only); composes with aie31.11 (owns WHEN a flow is admitted; this bead owns WHAT it stores + WHEN evicted); aie31.10 already closed (TARGET_PORTS keys on front tuple, so eviction indexes off FWD_FLOW.value.pod_ip, not TARGET_PORTS). Awaiting operator decision.
## critical-reviewer findings — findings-doc — mayor-aie31.21

**Verdict**: needs-discussion

**Confirmed findings** (must be true, evidence cited):
- [HIGH] "TCP self-heals via reset" and open-question-1's "correctness is identical either way" do not hold under the doc's own Option A model. A strictly-pinned flow never rehashes to a different backend, so no live host ever receives the packet to emit an RST; the doc's own UDP-mandatory rationale ("refreshes FWD_FLOW LRU recency on every packet, so LRU pressure alone never reclaims it") applies equally to a TCP flow retrying against the departed pod, since later packets hit-not-reinsert FWD_FLOW (doc's own Option A: "FWD_FLOW hit -> follow the stored pin, skip VIP_MAP resolution"). title: design(servicelb): unified flow table with an explicit role tag
description:
Merge FWD_FLOW and REV_FLOW into one table discriminated by an explicit tag
rather than by address disjointness, and settle the ceiling as part of it.

Measured on a live kernel via bpftool, so these are exact rather than
modelled. All LRU_HASH, bytes_memlock:

  forward map today, key 37 value 4, 8192 entries        918,400
  reverse map today, key 37 value 12, 8192 entries       983,936
  pair today                                           1,902,336
  unified, key 38 value 12, 4096 entries                 492,416
  unified, key 38 value 12, 8192 entries                 983,936
  unified, key 38 value 12, 16384 entries              1,966,976

The CI sampler total across all five servicelb maps is 1,909,072, leaving
6,736 for CONFIG, VIP_MAP, and POD_TARGETS.

The tag byte is free. BPF rounds key_size up to a multiple of 8 when sizing
elements, confirmed by measurement rather than by reading hashtab.c: key
sizes 36 through 40 all cost the same, and 41 jumps by exactly 8 bytes per
entry. See bd memory ebpf-map-key-size-rounds-up-to-8 for the numbers and the
reproduction method. That is why the unified 8192 row above is byte-identical
to today's reverse map on its own.

Alternative worth weighing and recording: the tag does not strictly need a
38th byte. The existing proto byte holds 6 or 17 and has six spare bits, so a
high bit could carry direction and a second bit QUIC, keeping the key at 37
and touching no call sites. The explicit byte is recommended anyway, since it
costs nothing and is self-documenting, but the choice should be written down.

Do NOT rest this on VIP-space versus pod-CIDR disjointness. That invariant
does not hold for hostNetwork Pods; see the disjointness bead. Note also that
the two maps carry different value types today, 4 bytes against 12, so the
tag has to select the value shape as well as the key population.

Capacity tradeoff to decide, not assume. Unifying at 8192 halves memory and
keeps full capacity for a single-role node, but halves worst-case capacity
for a node serving both roles. Unifying at 16384 costs 64,640 bytes more than
today and yields 16384 flexible slots instead of a fixed 8192 plus 8192,
which strictly dominates. Bucket arrays round to a power of two, so those are
the only sensible stops.

QUIC folds in as a third population under the same tag once native QUIC
lands, rather than needing a fourth map.

Also update ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md line 96, which states
the key as 37 bytes.

DONE WHEN: one tagged table exists, its value shape covers both roles, and
the ceiling choice is recorded with its reasoning.

title: perf(servicelb): release the aya object after attach so the DaemonSet idles thin
description:
Pin the maps, drop the aya Ebpf object after attach, trim the heap, and
reopen maps from their pins when they are next needed, so the DaemonSet
container idles thin instead of holding load-time state forever.

The blocking loop at src/main.rs:204 is correct and must stay. A DaemonSet
Pod only accepts restartPolicy Always, so exiting would be restarted and
eventually backed off. The cost is not the sleep, it is what the process
holds while sleeping. Ebpf::load parses the object at line 153 and keeps the
BTF, relocation state, and program registry alive for the whole process
lifetime, and the 214 KiB embedded blob is resident once touched. Glibc does
not return that heap on its own, so resident memory sits at the load-time
high-water mark, which in a container is what the memory request has to cover
on every node.

MapData::from_pin exists in aya 0.14 for reopening. Phase 5's watcher needs
map handles, not the parsed ELF.

Worth recording while here: since Linux 5.11, BPF map memory is charged to
the creating process's cgroup, so the roughly 1.82 MiB of map memory counts
against this container's own memory limit rather than sitting outside it. Map
sizing and container limits are one budget, not two. The bump_memlock_rlimit
call at src/main.rs:296 only matters for kernels older than that.

DONE WHEN: steady-state RSS in the existing loader-rss.csv sampler drops
measurably below the load-time peak, with the attachment still live.

title: perf(servicelb): make the per-packet flow-table writes conditional
description:
Replace the unconditional per-packet map inserts with
lookup-then-write-on-miss.

servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:238 inserts into FWD_FLOW on every forwarded
packet, and line 418 inserts into REV_FLOW on every decapped packet, not just
on the first packet of a flow. An LRU hash update takes the bucket
raw_spinlock and can run the LRU shrink path. A lookup is an RCU read that
already refreshes the entry's LRU reference bit, so recency is preserved
without the write. The difference is largest under multi-core load, where
several CPUs serialize on one bucket lock for a single busy flow.

FWD_FLOW's value is constant per flow, so skipping the rewrite is trivially
safe. REV_FLOW's value can legitimately change if the ingress node changes,
so the check there is exists-and-matches rather than plain existence.

DONE WHEN: steady-state packets of an established flow take the read path,
verified by a map-update counter that stays flat while traffic flows.

title: perf(servicelb): gate the egress conntrack lookup on POD_TARGETS membership
description:
Gate the uplink-egress conntrack lookup on POD_TARGETS membership, checking
only that the source address is a backend Pod on this node and deliberately
not comparing the port.

try_uplink_egress_return at servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:537 performs a
40-byte-key LRU hash lookup on every TCP and UDP packet leaving the node
before it can reject non-ServiceLB traffic. POD_TARGETS is a 32-entry map
with a 4-byte key, so probing it first is a far cheaper hash and it
short-circuits before the 37-byte key is even built on the stack.

Membership only, not a port match. Comparing the packet's source port against
the current POD_TARGETS value would couple the return path to a value that
can change under it during a rolling update or a targetPort change, dropping
live flows whose reverse entry was written under the old port. The current
code cannot produce that failure, because it matches purely on the stored
tuple. Membership is safe by construction: a flow only has a reverse entry if
the forward path found its pod in this map, so anything still live passes,
and a pod absent from the map is going away regardless.

Pairs with the REV_FLOW-miss bead, which needs exactly this positive
identification before it can safely turn a miss into a drop.

DONE WHEN: traffic not sourced from a backend Pod rejects without touching
the conntrack table, and a test covers that a targetPort change does not
break an in-flight flow.

title: perf(servicelb): direct packet access instead of bpf_skb_load_bytes on both uplink hooks
description:
Replace ctx.load with direct packet access on both uplink hooks, because
every ctx.load is a bpf_skb_load_bytes helper call and these hooks see all
node traffic, not just ServiceLB's.

Confirmed in aya-ebpf 0.2.1: TcContext::load delegates to SkBuff::load, which
calls bpf_skb_load_bytes. Cost per packet before either hook can even reject
non-ServiceLB traffic:

- try_uplink_egress_return, servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:537. Seven helper
  calls plus a 40-byte-key LRU hash lookup.
- try_uplink_ingress, servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:207. Five helper calls plus
  a VIP_MAP lookup.

That is paid by kubelet, etcd, image pulls, flannel, and everything else
entering or leaving the node. ctx.data and ctx.data_end are available in this
aya version, turning each read into a plain load behind one bounds check.
Adjacent fields can also coalesce: the source and destination addresses are
contiguous, as are the two ports.

Caution: direct packet access covers the linear head only. Headers are linear
in practice for tc ingress and for egress from a local socket, but any read
that reaches into a payload, which native QUIC will need for the DCID,
requires bpf_skb_pull_data or a load-bytes fallback.

This gets more valuable under the dual-stack and QUIC requirements, not less.
IPv6 means branching on ethertype with different header offsets and walking
extension headers, each of which is another helper call under the current
approach.

DONE WHEN: header reads go through ctx.data and ctx.data_end with
verifier-accepted bounds checks, and the servicelb smoke fixture still passes
end to end.

title: docs(ebpf-lb): correct the VIP-space vs pod-CIDR disjointness claim
description:
The claim that VIP-space and the pod CIDR are disjoint by construction is
false for hostNetwork Pods, and the doc uses it to justify a design choice.

ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md line 89 states the two ranges never
collide and concludes that one map per protocol can cover both the forward
and reverse roles. A Pod with hostNetwork true has a pod IP equal to its node
IP, which is exactly VIP space under the node-owned-address model. That is
standard Kubernetes semantics, not misconfiguration, and this repo already
ships two hostNetwork DaemonSets in manifests/kube-proxy.yaml and
manifests/flannel.yaml. The doc specifies the servicelb control plane itself
as hostNetwork at line 131.

Concrete collision, node N at 192.168.109.3. A forward key for a service
fronted at N holds N's address in its other-address slot. A reverse key for a
hostNetwork backend on N holds the same address in the same slot. A client
legally reusing one local port across both makes the two 37-byte keys
byte-identical.

The ranges are also only disjoint by configuration today, not by
construction. The pod CIDR is 10.244.0.0/16 from scripts/install.sh:890 and
node addresses sit on 192.168.x.x, set by unrelated mechanisms with no
cross-validation. The --vip-ip flag at src/main.rs:56 is an unvalidated
address with no check that it is the node's own or outside the pod CIDR.

Calibration note: the same paragraph of this doc was already wrong once,
specifying LRU_PERCPU_HASH, which was empirically disproved and corrected.
That is reason to audit the neighbouring sentence rather than defer to it.

Consider merging with aie31.3, which corrects the map type and footprint in
the same file. Kept separate here because this one also needs a code change.

DONE WHEN: the doc states the real constraint rather than a false invariant,
and the loader rejects a VIP that falls inside the pod CIDR.

title: design(servicelb): aie31.21 eviction ignores cross-node convergence drift - delivery node must be the authoritative consistency point
description: Operator raised 2026-09-07: the aie31.21 affinity+eviction doc reasons about eviction as a per-node reconcile but never addresses the cross-node convergence WINDOW. Each node's DaemonSet processes the same EndpointSlice event at different times (uplink latency), so node eBPF state can drift apart for multiple seconds before converging. Governing principle to add to the doc: dataplane is eventually-consistent per node; correctness must NOT depend on synchronized updates; worst case during the window must be bounded transient drop/hang, NEVER misdelivery to a wrong live pod. Scenarios: new-flow selection divergence = safe (per-flow ECMP-sticky to one ingress node); stale FWD_FLOW pin during removal lag = blackhole/hang if IP not reused (bounded, ok) BUT misdelivery if the departed pod's IP is reused before the lagging ingress node evicts (UNSAFE - the drift window widens this). RESOLVING INVARIANT: make the delivery (backend-host) node validate each inbound Geneve-decap packet against its OWN current serving-set for the front IP before delivering - the host has a lag-free view of its local pods, so ingress drift degrades to a drop at the authoritative node, not a cross-service leak. OPEN QUESTION to verify against code: does the inbound decap-forward delivery path in crates/servicelb/servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs currently do this membership check? aie31.14 gates EGRESS on POD_TARGETS (different hook) - may not cover inbound delivery. Action: amend aie31.21 doc with the cross-node-drift section + invariant; file a build bead if the delivery-side validation is missing. Part of parked aie31 epic.
notes: Verdict: invariant does NOT hold today. try_geneve_decap_forward (servicelb-ebpf/src/main.rs:331-471) trusts the ingress-stamped Geneve pod_ip unconditionally and DNATs to it; its only check, TARGET_PORTS.get(front tuple) (main.rs:361-368), validates "this node serves some backend for this front", not "this pod_ip is a current member" -- no analogue of aie31.14's egress POD_TARGETS-membership gate exists on the inbound decap-delivery path. Drift verdict: new-flow divergence is SAFE (per-flow ECMP-sticky); stale FWD_FLOW pin without IP reuse is SAFE (bounded blackhole/hang); stale pin WITH pod-IP reuse before the lagging ingress evicts is UNSAFE -- misdelivers to the new pod, and the drift window directly widens this exposure. Doc amended: ai/findings/2026-09-06-mayor-aie31.21-affinity-pinning-eviction.md, new "Cross-node convergence & drift" section (keeps its aie31.21 header, doc-only PR under mayor-1dwwz). title: docs(ebpf-lb): correct the LB-minted QUIC CID premise (CID is server/backend-chosen per RFC 9000 7.2, not LB-minted)
description: g3lag + aie31.11 research (2026-09-06) both found that ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md (approx lines 99-111, 160) describes the routing Connection ID as minted by the LB. That premise is false for a non-terminating tc-bpf dataplane: per RFC 9000 section 7.2 the CID is server-chosen, and post-handshake CIDs travel in encrypted NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames; the 1-RTT short header omits CID length (section 17.3.1). The only cooperation model is backend-generated routable CIDs the LB decodes (draft-ietf-quic-load-balancers), which requires backend opt-in and is Envoy-only today. Correct the doc so the CID claim reflects server/backend-chosen CIDs, and align the QUIC-exempt admission narrative. title: net/servicelb: decide eBPF tc-bpf hook topology accounting for future TPROXY return-leg reuse -- single hook vs separate hooks, kernel perf and memory
description: L3 hook-topology design decision for the eBPF ServiceLB dataplane. A future L7 tier might reuse the existing symmetric-Geneve return path via TPROXY; account for that now when placing the tc-bpf hooks. If one hook point can safely and efficiently serve both ingress classification and a future TPROXY return leg, that is beneficial; if separate hooks are significantly cheaper on kernel memory or processing, that is fine too -- eBPF runs in-kernel, so this must be designed deliberately, not retrofitted. Kernel constraint to capture: node-local-originated traffic, for example a same-node proxy dialing the local node IP or VIP, is delivered by local routing and does not traverse the physical-NIC tc ingress qdisc, so a single hook on the physical uplink alone cannot serve the TPROXY return leg without an added local or loopback-aware hook. See the new Hook topology design note in ai/extended-context/ebpf-lb-dataplane.md. Stays on the aie31 L3 dataplane track; not a commitment to build L7 TPROXY.
notes:
Findings: ai/findings/2026-09-06-mayor-bguco-tc-bpf-hook-topology.md (branch worker/agent-ab570063b274c4d03, no PR).
